title: The plain meeting house
hook: Quaker and Puritan rooms of white walls and clear glass

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gothic cathedral: stone lifted high, walls turned into colored glass. Your line was stone reaching up. Where did your eyes climb yesterday? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

White walls. Clear glass. Wooden benches. No statues, no painted windows, no altar. In a Quaker meeting house the benches may face each other across the room, and there may be no pulpit at all. People come in, sit down, and the room goes quiet. Nobody announces a hymn. Nobody reads a set prayer. A clock ticks. Outside the plain window, a branch moves. After a long while, someone stands, says a few sentences, and sits down. The quiet comes back. In an old New England meeting house built by Puritans, the room is just as bare, but everything turns toward a high pulpit where the Bible is read and preached. Two plain rooms, built that way on purpose. Today: the plain meeting house.

Yesterday's cathedral and today's meeting house come from the same Bible. They answer different questions. The cathedral asks how a building can lift the eye toward God. The meeting house asks what might stand in the way. Start with the building itself. In Athens, Paul tells a crowd standing among temples: "God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands." Christians who built plain leaned hard on that line. The room is only a room. It shelters the people, and that's its job. Next, the worship. Jesus tells a Samaritan woman at a well, "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." Puritans wanted worship stripped back to what they found in scripture, so the Bible, read and preached, stands at the center. Quakers went another way into the same plainness. They speak of the light of Christ within each person, and they hear it in John's Gospel: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." So in a Quaker meeting of the silent kind, anyone may rise and speak, and no one has to. Then, the people. "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." In this reading, the holy center of the room is the gathering itself. And last, the clear glass. No saints in the window, just the real sky and the real tree. Nothing between. On the mountain, Elijah learns that the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire. After the fire came "a still small voice."
screen: `DWELLETH NOT IN TEMPLES MADE WITH HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in a plain room. Find the barest spot you can, a blank wall, an empty table, a window with nothing on the sill. Sit down and let there be nothing to look at and nothing to do. Breathe. When a thought arrives, let it pass like a car outside. If you pray, you can wait the way a Quaker meeting waits, without asking for anything, listening for a still small voice. If you don't, simply sit in the quiet and let the plainness be enough. The bell holds the time.
The plain meeting house. A room kept bare on purpose, white walls and clear glass, so that nothing stands between the gathered people and God.
Your line: nothing between. Today, clear one surface, a desk, a counter, a windowsill, and leave it empty until evening. Notice how it changes the room. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: In unprogrammed Quaker meetings, people gather in a plain room and sit in silence, and anyone may rise to speak when moved; churches in the Puritan and Reformed line gather in plain rooms centered on the reading and preaching of the Bible.

notes: Quaker meetings described as 'of the silent kind' (unprogrammed); programmed Quaker meetings with pastors also exist. Confirm the framing is fair.
'They speak of the light of Christ within each person, and they hear it in John's Gospel' (John 1:9): confirm this is a fair account of Quaker usage without overstating.
New England Puritan meeting houses described as plain and turned toward a high pulpit; general, undated. Confirm.
Hebrew of 1 Kings 19:12 (qol demamah daqqah) and transliteration should be checked.
The cathedral/meeting-house contrast is framed as two answers to different questions, neither ranked; confirm it reads that way.

Editor: fixed a garbled sentence; reworded so cathedral builders are not implied to take scripture less seriously; Elijah line now follows 1 Kings 19 (the text says the LORD was not in wind, earthquake or fire, then the voice came) instead of saying God was found in the voice.
